design_detail: Ecological controlled before–after (difference-in-differences) analysis of US vital statistics (CDC Compressed Mortality Files: underlying cause of death, coded in ICD-8 for 1968–1978 and ICD-9 for 1979–1998), aggregated by state. Intervention: a state's switch from a coroner, justice-of-the-peace or mixed system to a medical examiner system, with dates from Hanzlick and Combs (1998). Of nine states that switched between 1970 and 1996, seven were analysed (West Virginia, Arizona and New Mexico 1976; New Jersey 1978; Massachusetts 1983; New Hampshire 1986; Alaska 1996); Delaware and Florida (1970) were dropped for lack of pre-switch years. Each was paired with one control state that stayed coroner or mixed, chosen for proximity and visually similar pre-switch trends in the outcome (Ohio, Idaho, New York, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Indiana, Montana). Outcome: the yearly share of solid and liquid poisoning deaths (drugs and other substances) whose underlying-cause code was non-specific. Ordinary least-squares model with a group indicator, a before/after indicator and their interaction, fitted on all years (N = 429 state-years), on 7 years before to 10 after the switch (N = 236) and on 7 before to 5 after (N = 176). Single author, public-policy department. Filed as registry (vital-statistics data) and appraised with ROBINS-I as a non-randomized comparison of an intervention, as the round brief directs.
can_establish: Whether, in seven US states that adopted medical examiner systems between 1976 and 1996, the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code fell more after the switch than in seven matched states that kept coroner or mixed systems, within the precision these data allow.
cannot_establish: Whether medical examiner systems name drugs more specifically on certificates in the ICD-10 era (the outcome uses underlying-cause codes only, includes non-drug poisonings and ends in 1998); whether reform has no effect (the intervals include falls of 10 to 14 percentage points from a baseline near one half); or whether individual certifiers matter more than systems, for which the paper offers only anecdotes.

sample.recruitment: Registry: CDC Compressed Mortality Files, county-level underlying cause of death 1968–2016, of which 1968–1998 were analysed at state level (p. 2, Section 2, Materials and methods, 1st paragraph; footnote 2, p. 4). Switching states from Hanzlick and Combs (1998) (Table 1, p. 2); controls from states that stayed coroner or mixed throughout (pp. 2–3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Nine states switched in 1970–1996; Delaware and Florida (1970) were excluded because only two pre-switch years exist, and controls were matched on geographic proximity and approximately parallel pre-switch trends in the outcome, searching further afield when no neighbouring state matched (pp. 2–3, Section 2, 3rd paragraph). Four state-year values above 1.00 were removed; none lay within a decade of a switch (p. 3, Section 2, 6th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (aggregate state data). The numbers of poisoning deaths behind each state-year share are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Alaska has only two post-switch years, 1997 and 1998 (p. 4, Results 1st paragraph and footnote 2).
sample.selection_effects: Seven switches, all before 1999, in states the author says already had many characteristics of medical examiner states (p. 5, Discussion 6th paragraph). Controls were picked by the author from visual similarity of trends, without a stated rule. Whether control states had county-level switches of their own (said to have continued into the 1990s, p. 2) is not checked. Two switches replaced physicians (Massachusetts: physician coroner; New Hampshire: locally appointed physician), so the lay-coroner contrast that motivates the study does not apply to them.

exposure.measurement: The intervention is the state's switch to a medical examiner system, dated from Hanzlick and Combs (1998) (Table 1, p. 2). Previous systems: justices of the peace (West Virginia, Arizona), coroner (New Mexico, New Jersey), physician coroner (Massachusetts), locally appointed physician (New Hampshire), magistrate coroner (Alaska). Resulting systems: centralized medical examiner (West Virginia, New Mexico, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Alaska) or decentralized medical examiner (Arizona, New Jersey). Control states' systems are described only as coroner or mixed.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (one underlying-cause code per death).

comparison.controls: Seven control states that kept coroner or mixed systems, one per switching state.
comparison.matching: Pairs (Table 2, p. 3): New Hampshire–Ohio, New Mexico–Idaho, New Jersey–New York, Massachusetts–Pennsylvania, Arizona–Nevada, West Virginia–Indiana, Alaska–Montana, chosen by proximity and by the pre-switch trend of the outcome, on the assumption that this controls for other relevant variables. A synthetic control was considered and rejected because the literature identifies no predictors of certificate specificity (pp. 3–4, Section 2.1, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. State characteristics the author names as possible common causes or mediators (population density, political culture, regulatory structure, autopsy facilities, certifiers' training, staff carried over from the old system) are not measured (pp. 4–5, Discussion 3rd to 6th paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: Share (u/t) of solid and liquid poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code, by the ICD codes of Table 3 (pp. 3–4). Non-specific (u): ICD-8 E859.9, E869, E950.3, E950.9, E980.3, E980.9; ICD-9 E858.9, E866.9, E950.5, E950.9, E980.5, E980.9. All (t): accidental poisoning by drugs and medicaments (ICD-8 E850–E859; ICD-9 E850–E858) plus the suicide and undetermined-intent solid and liquid poisoning codes (E950.0–E950.9, E980.0–E980.9).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated. Because the older codes cannot separate drug overdoses from other solid or liquid poisonings, all were included (p. 3, Section 2, 5th paragraph); multiple-cause data, needed for the drug-specification measures of the cross-sectional studies, exist only from 1999 (p. 3, Section 2, 4th paragraph). The ICD-9 revision of 1979 separated 'other specified' from 'unspecified' substances and produced sharp falls in the share in switching and control states alike (p. 4, Results 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Improved data quality = a smaller non-specific share after the switch, relative to the control state (the interaction term).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None needed for one outcome; the same interaction was estimated in three overlapping windows, all non-significant.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 4 (p. 5): difference-in-differences estimate −0.02 (SE 0.04) in the all-years model, −0.03 (0.05) with 10 post-switch years and −0.02 (0.06) with 5; none significant. Before/after ('Year') coefficients −0.23, −0.18 and −0.14 (all p < 0.05), attributed to the ICD-9 change; group coefficients −0.04, −0.01, −0.01; intercepts 0.53, 0.50, 0.50; R² 0.29, 0.20, 0.11; residual standard error 0.19 to 0.20; N 429, 236, 176. The author calls the estimates a 2%–3% impact on rates (p. 4); on the proportion scale they are 2 to 3 percentage points. Editors' calculation (estimate ± 1.96 SE): 95% intervals −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07 and −0.14 to 0.10, compatible with falls in the non-specific share of up to 10 to 14 percentage points from about 0.50, and with rises of up to 6 to 10 points.
analysis.covariates: None. No state or calendar-year fixed effects; ordinary least-squares standard errors, with no stated allowance for repeated observations of the same state.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol. The second stated objective, quantifying the change, was dropped because no change was found (p. 2, Section 1.2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Estimates for each pair are not reported, although Figure 1 suggests the pairs differ: after the switch New Jersey stays well above New York, while New Mexico, West Virginia and Massachusetts lie below their controls (values not extracted). All three pooled models are reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With seven switching states and the intervals above, moderate effects could not be excluded (editors' reading).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In seven state switches between 1976 and 1996, the non-specific share of poisoning deaths' underlying-cause codes did not fall detectably more than in seven matched states (estimates −0.02 to −0.03, SE 0.04 to 0.06); the intervals include sizeable improvements as well as small deteriorations.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the research finds no evidence that system-level reform is associated with better drug-related mortality data, which is accurate as a statement of non-significance. The Discussion goes further, saying reform “did not result in improved public health data” on drug-related mortality (p. 4, Discussion 1st paragraph), and the Conclusion says reform was not associated with the expected increase (p. 6), reading absence of evidence as evidence of absence. The outcome is called drug-related mortality data, but it includes non-drug poisonings, uses underlying-cause codes only and ends in 1998. The recommendation to focus on individual certifiers and offices rather than systems (abstract; p. 6, Conclusion) rests on unsourced anecdotes, not on analysis.

timeline.event: Hanzlick and Combs, history and trends of medical examiner and coroner systems: the source of the switch dates (reference 14).

Warner et al. (cross-sectional): drugs specified on 92% of certificates in centralized medical examiner states, 71% in decentralized medical examiner states, 73% in hybrid states and 62% in coroner states (reference 3, as cited, p. 2).
Fernandez (working paper): states that changed to a medical examiner system reported suicides more accurately, using longitudinal data (reference 4, as cited, pp. 2 and 4).
This study: no detectable change in the non-specific share of poisoning underlying-cause codes after seven state switches, 1976–1996.

Smiley-McDonald et al.: in the 2018 census, about 80% of US offices were within a coroner system, and coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which cases received toxicology (card sc_smiley_mcdonald_2025, this reader).

Lundberg et al.: within the same state and year, drug poisoning deaths in coroner counties were recorded as of undetermined intent more often than in medical examiner counties (nine states, 2019–2021; card sc_lundberg_2026).

replication.where_it_stands: The only longitudinal test of system reform for poisoning or drug-death data on the project's list. It does not overturn the cross-sectional associations (Warner et al., 2013, as cited; Lundberg et al., 2026), because its outcome, era and precision differ from theirs. Whether a switch to a medical examiner system changes how specifically drugs are named on certificates in the ICD-10 era remains untested.

funding.funder: No specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (p. 6, Funding; repeated under Declaration of competing interest).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author reports no competing interests (p. 6, Conflicts of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Public Policy and Political Economy, University of Texas at Dallas; current affiliation National Knowledge and Research Center for Emergency Preparedness, University of Haifa (p. 1). No interest in either kind of system is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: A difference-in-differences or synthetic-control study of recent county or state switches from coroner to medical examiner systems in the ICD-10 era, using multiple-cause data on whether certificates name specific drugs (T36–T50.8 against T50.9 alone), toxicology completeness and undetermined intent, with state and year fixed effects, standard errors clustered by jurisdiction, controls chosen by a stated rule and enough switching units to exclude a change of a few percentage points.

domains.note: A pooled two-group comparison with no covariates and no state or calendar-year fixed effects; controls matched only by visual pre-trend; parallel pre-switch trends are not tested and look doubtful for New Hampshire–Ohio and Alaska–Montana (Figure 1); the 1979 ICD-9 revision, which produced the largest changes in the data, falls inside the all-years model and inside the windows of five of the seven pairs (all but New Hampshire, whose window begins in 1979, and Alaska).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Seven of nine switching states (two dropped for too few pre-switch years); one control per state chosen by the author without a stated rule; four state-years removed for values above 1.00.

Switch dates from a 1998 secondary source; heterogeneous switches (justices of the peace, lay coroners, physician coroners or appointed physicians to centralized or decentralized medical examiners); control states' own systems and any county-level switches within them are not documented.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: The author notes that staff, facilities and oversight may have carried over, so some switches may have been changes of title only (p. 4); how fully each switch was implemented is unknown.
Complete vital statistics; four state-years removed outside the 10-year windows; the all-years N (429) is one fewer than expected (430), without explanation.

Underlying-cause codes only; non-drug poisonings included; the numerator contains accidental non-drug codes (E869, E866.9) that the denominator lacks, so the share is not a true proportion; the coding scheme changed during the study. Error of this kind probably affects switching and control states alike and would push the estimate toward no difference.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; the analysis windows and the controls were chosen by the author; all three pooled models are reported, but pair-specific results are not.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I, because the paper estimates the effect of an intervention (switching to a medical examiner system) without randomization. Two domains are serious: confounding, from a pooled model without fixed effects and a coding revision inside most windows; and outcome measurement, from a measure that mixes non-drug poisonings, uses underlying causes only and is not a true proportion. Apart from bias, the estimates are imprecise, and ordinary standard errors on repeated state-years probably make them look more precise than they are. Citable for: in seven state switches from 1976 to 1996, no detectable change in the non-specific share of poisoning underlying-cause codes relative to matched states, with intervals that cannot exclude a fall of 10 to 14 percentage points; the code lists used; the sharp fall in non-specific coding at the 1979 ICD-9 revision. Not citable for: 'medical examiner systems do not improve drug-death data', effects in the ICD-10 era, effects on the naming of specific drugs, or the claim that individual certifiers matter more than systems.

key_findings.finding: The research question: does switching from a coroner to a medical examiner system improve public health data on drug-related mortality? The author notes that cross-sectional studies had linked data quality to system type, and that no longitudinal study had tested this for drug deaths.
key_findings.locator: Section 1.2, Research question and objectives, 1st paragraph; Section 1.1, Background, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nine states switched to medical examiner systems between 1970 and 1996 (Table 1): Delaware 1970 (coroner with state medical examiner to centralized), Florida 1970 (justices of the peace to decentralized), West Virginia 1976 (justices of the peace to centralized), Arizona 1976 (justices of the peace to decentralized), New Mexico 1976 (coroner to centralized), New Jersey 1978 (coroner to decentralized), Massachusetts 1983 (physician coroner to centralized), New Hampshire 1986 (locally appointed physician to centralized) and Alaska 1996 (magistrate coroner to centralized).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Section 2, Materials and methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Delaware and Florida were excluded (only two pre-switch years); the remaining seven were paired with controls chosen for proximity and parallel pre-switch trends in non-specific poisoning (Table 2: New Hampshire–Ohio, New Mexico–Idaho, New Jersey–New York, Massachusetts–Pennsylvania, Arizona–Nevada, West Virginia–Indiana, Alaska–Montana).
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 2, continues p. 3); Table 2 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Because multiple-cause data exist only from 1999 and the older codes cannot isolate drug overdoses, the outcome is the share of all solid and liquid poisoning deaths (drug and non-drug) whose underlying-cause code is non-specific, with the codes listed in Table 3.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 3); Table 3 (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: After shares were calculated for the fourteen states over 31 years, four state-year values above 1.00 were removed; the author states that all non-specific codes are included in the all-poisoning category and that it is not clear why this occurred; none of these values lay within a decade of a switch.
key_findings.note: Table 3 itself lists E869 (ICD-8) and E866.9 (ICD-9) among the non-specific codes but not among the all-poisoning codes, which would allow values above 1.00 (editors' reading of Table 3).

key_findings.finding: The model was Y = β0 + β1·Year + β2·Group + β3·Year×Group, with Year a before/after indicator and the interaction as the effect, fitted on all observations, on 7 years before and 10 after, and on 7 before and 5 after the switch; the author considers the two windowed models better measures of the switch's effect.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 7th and 8th paragraphs (the one-line paragraph introducing the equation, and the paragraph after it)

key_findings.finding: Difference-in-differences estimates were −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (SE 0.05) and −0.02 (SE 0.06) in the all-years, 10-year and 5-year models (N 429, 236, 176), none statistically significant; the before/after coefficients were −0.23, −0.18 and −0.14 (p < 0.05), which the author attributes to the ICD-9 change.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of 95% intervals: −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10. The windowed Ns reproduce only if the switch year is included in each window (7 + 1 + 10 and 7 + 1 + 5 years, with Alaska and Montana contributing 10 years each); the all-years N is one fewer than 14 × 31 − 4 = 430 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 shows each pair from 7 years before to 10 years after the switch: in the first four pairs, shares fell sharply in both switching and control states when ICD-9 took effect (in the Massachusetts–Pennsylvania pair the same fall comes before the switch), because ICD-9 separated 'other specified' from 'unspecified' substances.
key_findings.note: Values not extracted from the figure. Read on a 300-dpi rendering: after the switch, New Jersey stays well above New York, while New Mexico, West Virginia and Massachusetts lie below their controls; New Hampshire lies above Ohio before and after.

key_findings.finding: A county-level analysis was intended but abandoned because counts of unspecified drug deaths are too low at county level.
key_findings.locator: Section 2.1, A note on synthetic controls, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Second-hand figures in the Background: in a frequently cited study, drugs were specified on 92% of death certificates in centralized medical examiner states, 71% in decentralized medical examiner states, 73% in hybrid states and 62% in coroner states (Warner et al., reference 3); and a 2004 report found that offices serving more than 250,000 people performed toxicology in drug intoxication deaths in 57% of cases, against 34% in offices serving fewer.
key_findings.note: As cited (references 3 and 9: Warner et al. 2013, Academic Forensic Pathology; the BJS census report for 2004); not read.

key_findings.finding: Context in the Introduction and Background: medical examiners or coroners certify unnatural or unusual deaths, about 20% of US mortality; a 2009 National Academy of Sciences report counted 2,342 separate death investigation jurisdictions; the author classes current states as 17 centralized medical examiner, 6 decentralized medical examiner, 19 hybrid and 14 coroner.
key_findings.locator: Section 1, Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Section 1.1, Background, 2nd paragraph (p. 2)
key_findings.note: The four state counts sum to 56, without explanation (editors' arithmetic); Smiley-McDonald et al. (2025, p. 542) give 16 states with centralized offices.

key_findings.finding: Discussion examples of state practice: in New Mexico, 88.8% of drug poisoning deaths filed in 2013–2017 carried T50.9 (other and unspecified drugs) but only 2.9% carried T50.9 alone, because certifiers there add T50.9 to specifically named drugs in case other drugs were missed; Maryland recorded 85% of drug deaths as of undetermined intent, against 1% to 30% in most states (Warner et al.).
key_findings.note: The New Mexico figures have no cited source.

key_findings.finding: Anecdotes offered for the role of individual officials: after a board-certified forensic pathologist was elected coroner of Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, in 2007, use of T50.9 in drug deaths fell by over 60 percentage points within two years, and Franklin, Ohio, saw a similar fall after the 2008 election of a forensic pathologist as coroner.
key_findings.note: No source is cited for either figure.

key_findings.finding: The author's conclusion: the longitudinal analysis failed to confirm the cross-sectional association; system reform was not associated with the expected improvement; specific, likely narrow mechanisms focused on individual certifying officials and offices should be identified instead of system-wide regulation.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 contradicts the statement that all non-specific codes are included among all poisoning codes: the non-specific list includes E869 (ICD-8) and E866.9 (ICD-9), accidental poisoning by other or unspecified solid or liquid substances, while the all-poisoning list includes only accidental poisoning by drugs (E850–E859; E850–E858).
reporting_issues.consequence: The share can exceed 1.00, as it did in four state-years the author could not explain; accidental non-drug poisonings enter the numerator only, adding measurement error that may vary between states and over time.

reporting_issues.issue: The all-years model has N = 429, one fewer than 14 states × 31 years minus 4 removed values (430); the windowed Ns (236, 176) reproduce only if the switch year is counted inside each window, which the methods do not say (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the analysis cannot be reproduced exactly from the description.

reporting_issues.issue: The model description calls Group a county indicator and the Results refer to control and experimental counties, although the analysis is by state; the before/after indicator is named Year; the sentence defining Y is incomplete ('either the rate of unspecified drug deaths').
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take the analysis for county-level; it is state-level throughout.

reporting_issues.issue: The estimates −0.02 to −0.03 are described as a 2%–3% impact on rates; on the proportion scale they are 2 to 3 percentage points, about 4% to 6% of a baseline share near 0.50 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the estimate is understated in relative terms; either way it is imprecise.

reporting_issues.issue: Standard errors are ordinary least squares on 176 to 429 state-years from 14 states, with no stated allowance for repeated observations of the same state.
reporting_issues.consequence: The true uncertainty is probably wider than the printed standard errors, which strengthens the point that moderate effects cannot be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The Montgomery County and Franklin falls in T50.9 use (over 60 percentage points) and New Mexico's 88.8% and 2.9% are given without sources.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be checked and should not be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The title, abstract and conclusion speak of drug-related mortality data, but the measure includes non-drug solid and liquid poisonings (for example arsenic, strychnine, lye, corrosives and agricultural chemicals in Table 3) and uses underlying causes only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The result concerns the specificity of poisoning codes in 1968–1998, not how specifically certificates named drugs.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's title says 1968–2016 but its source is from 1998; the Background's state counts (17, 6, 19, 14) sum to 56.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; switches after 1998, if any, would not appear in the source.
